newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Cyprus approves aid package for trade, tourism.
newsitem.headline: Cyprus approves aid package for trade, tourism.

text.p: Cyprus on Wednesday announced an 11 million pound ($22.4 million) government cash injection to boost industrial exports and promote tourism.
The government also said it wanted lower interest rates.

"(We have decided for the) adoption of the Central Bank proposal for the reduction of interest rates after consultations, which are already under way with the commercial banks and the cooperative movement," Finance Minister Christodoulos Christodoulou told reporters after a cabinet meeting.
He added the reduction would be accompanied by steps to ensure that it did not lead to excessive private consumption.

Banks now officially charge the public 8.5 percent for loans. A nine percent interest rate ceiling has been in place in Cyprus since 1944, when Cyprus was a British colony. The government says it is committed to scrapping the ceiling before entry talks start with the European Union next year.

The Central Bank of Cyprus lowered its lending rate to commercial banks to 7.0 percent from 7.5 percent, and its overnight deposit rate to 4.0 percent from 5.0 percent last month, in a signal for the banks to lower their retail rates.
Christodoulou said four million pounds will be allocated to promote industrial exports, with emphasis placed on assisting clothing, footwear, leather and baggage manufacturers.
An additional 3.5 million pounds will be spent this year on promoting tourism, the eastern Mediterranean island's main money spinner.
Tourism represents 21 percent of Cyprus's gross domestic product, but travel statistics released earlier in the week indicate a 6.4 percent decline in arrivals in 1996 over 1995.
"We plan to speed up implementation of a plan for the subsidy of the interest (on loans) for the renovation of hotels with 1.5 million pounds," said Christodoulou.
He said two million pounds will be allocated to agriculture to compensate for damages incurred during the drought which continues to affect the island.
